content: An ancillary statistic in the field of statistics is defined as a statistic whose probability distribution remains unaffected by the specific probability distribution of the statistical population from which the data were sampled. This concept was first introduced by the renowned statistical geneticist Sir Ronald Fisher. For example, consider a set of independent and identically distributed random variables ( X_1, X_2, dots, X_n ), which follow a normal distribution with an expected value ( mu ) and a variance of 1. The sample mean, the interquartile range (( Q_3 Q_1 )), and the sample variance are all examples of ancillary statistics. This is because their probability distributions do not change as the value of ( mu ) varies. To illustrate the concept further, let us consider an example from baseball. Suppose a scout observes a batter over ( N ) at-bats. Assume, for simplicity, that the number ( N ) is determined by a random process independent of the batter's ability—for instance, a coin is flipped after each at-bat to decide whether the scout will stay to observe the next at-bat. The resulting data consist of the number of at-bats (( N )) and the number of hits (( X )). In this scenario, the number of at-bats (( N )) qualifies as an ancillary statistic. This is because: 1. It is part of the observable data, making it a statistic. 2. Its probability distribution is independent of the batter's ability, as ( N ) is determined by a random process unrelated to the batter's performance. However, the batting average (( X/N )) is not a sufficient statistic on its own, as it does not encapsulate all the relevant information contained in the data. When combined with ( N ), however, it becomes sufficient, as the pair (( X, N )) provides a complete summary of the data.
